author: A Robot
objectives: Describe Mars’s apparent retrograde path in the night sky, including normal eastward drift, westward reversal, and return to eastward motion.
Explain retrograde motion in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower outer planet.
Contrast geocentric epicycle-based explanations with the simpler heliocentric explanation.
Predict when retrograde motion occurs for an outer planet based on the relative orbital positions of Earth and the planet.
Compare retrograde loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and relate loop size to planetary distance.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: Mars in the Night Sky
modules.description: Students observe Mars tracing an apparent retrograde loop against zodiac constellations over several months.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the eastward drift, reversal, and resumed eastward motion of Mars.
Recognize retrograde motion as an apparent change relative to fixed background stars.
Describe why the observed loop became a major historical puzzle in astronomy.
instructions: Look toward the tabletop star dome and follow the red Mars marker as time fast-forwards.
Use Next and Previous to review the phases of the retrograde loop.
Pay attention to the labeled zodiac constellations that remain fixed while Mars moves.

components.text: Leo   Virgo   Libra   Scorpio
Observed Retrograde Motion of Mars

clips.changeMeaning: Initial staging presents the fixed star background and places Mars at the start of its normal eastward drift so students anchor on the observational frame.
clips.narration: Ancient skywatchers noticed that Mars usually drifts slowly eastward against the background constellations. In this scene, the stars stay fixed while Mars changes position night after night.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars advances eastward relative to the labeled zodiac constellations, establishing the ordinary motion seen before retrograde begins.
clips.narration: Over the first part of the sequence, Mars moves eastward, or prograde, across the ecliptic constellations. This slow drift is its usual apparent motion in the night sky.

clips.changeMeaning: The trail appears and Mars slows near its stationary point, preparing students to notice that the direction of motion is about to reverse.
clips.narration: Then Mars slows nearly to a halt. This turning point is called a stationary point, and it marks the beginning of the retrograde episode.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is moved backward across the starfield while the visible trail expands, making the westward loop visually explicit against the fixed constellations.
clips.narration: For about two months, Mars appears to reverse direction and move westward. Traced over time, its path forms a loop roughly fifteen degrees across.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars completes the loop and resumes eastward motion, leaving the full path visible so students can inspect the entire apparent retrograde pattern.
clips.narration: After the loop, Mars slows again, reverses once more, and resumes its usual eastward drift. This backward motion was one of the great puzzles that any successful model of the cosmos had to explain.

modules.description: Students see how a geocentric deferent-and-epicycle construction can reproduce retrograde motion.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the roles of the deferent and epicycle in the geocentric model.
Explain how combined circular motions can generate an apparent backward loop.
Recognize why the geocentric explanation required increasing complexity to match observations.
instructions: Watch Mars ride on a small epicycle whose center moves along a larger deferent around Earth.
Notice that retrograde occurs when Mars is on the inner side of the epicycle closest to Earth.
Compare the model’s explanatory power with its complexity.

components.text: Deferent
Epicycle

clips.changeMeaning: The geocentric machinery is presented in a simple initial configuration so students can identify Earth, the deferent, the epicycle, and Mars’s starting point.
clips.narration: In the geocentric model, Earth stands at the center. Mars moves on a small circle called an epicycle, while the center of that epicycle moves along a larger circle called the deferent.

clips.changeMeaning: The epicycle center shifts along the deferent while Mars also advances around the smaller circle, illustrating the combined circular motions used to fit observations.
clips.narration: By combining these two circular motions, astronomers could make Mars speed up, slow down, and even reverse direction as seen from Earth.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is moved to the inner side of the epicycle nearest Earth, showing the special configuration in which the apparent motion can become westward.
clips.narration: When Mars reaches the inner part of its epicycle, the motion from the small circle can temporarily outweigh the motion around the large circle. To an observer on Earth, Mars then appears to move backward.

components.text: Epicycle (tuned for fit)
Deferent (tuned for fit)

clips.changeMeaning: The labels are updated to stress that the circles and speeds had to be finely adjusted, connecting the visual model to its historical lack of parsimony.
clips.narration: The geocentric model could reproduce the loop, but only by carefully tuning circle sizes and speeds. As observations improved, more epicycles were often added, making the system increasingly complicated.

modules.description: Students view Earth and Mars orbiting the Sun and see retrograde emerge naturally when Earth overtakes Mars.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: State the relative orbital distances and speeds of Earth and Mars.
Explain why overtaking on an inner, faster orbit creates apparent retrograde motion.
Recognize that the heliocentric model uses smooth orbital motion rather than epicycles.
instructions: View the solar system from above the orbital plane.
Watch Earth move faster on the inner orbit and notice when it overtakes Mars.
Connect the overtaking event to the retrograde episode seen in the first scene.

components.text: Earth: 1 AU, 1 year | Mars: 1.52 AU, 1.88 years

clips.changeMeaning: The scene establishes the Sun-centered geometry and the different orbital radii of Earth and Mars before any overtaking occurs.
clips.narration: Now we rise above the solar system. The Sun is at the center, Earth orbits at one astronomical unit in one year, and Mars orbits farther out at about one point five two astronomical units in about one point eight eight years.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth advances more quickly around the Sun and begins to line up with Mars, setting up the overtaking geometry responsible for retrograde.
clips.narration: Because Earth is on the smaller orbit, it moves faster. Over time, Earth catches up to Mars from the inside track.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth moves past Mars in orbital longitude, making the key overtaking event explicit while both planets still follow smooth paths around the Sun.
clips.narration: At the crucial moment, Earth overtakes Mars. Nothing loops in space itself—both planets continue in smooth heliocentric orbits.

components.text: Retrograde arises from relative motion, not epicycles

clips.changeMeaning: After the pass, the planets continue smoothly onward and the text shifts emphasis from orbital numbers to the explanatory simplicity of the heliocentric model.
clips.narration: After Earth passes Mars, the apparent retrograde episode ends. The heliocentric model explains the same observation with a simpler idea: relative motion between planets on different orbits.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Linking Line of Sight to the Sky Loop
modules.description: Students see the outside view and Earth-sky view together, linked by a sweeping Earth-to-Mars line of sight.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Connect the heliocentric geometry to the apparent motion seen against the stars.
Explain how the line of sight reverses direction during overtaking.
Distinguish real apparent motion from physical looping motion in space.
instructions: Compare the left heliocentric panel and right sky panel.
Follow the line drawn from Earth through Mars to the background stars.
Notice that the apparent reversal in the sky occurs exactly when the line of sight reverses.

components.text: Geometry links the two views

clips.changeMeaning: Both perspectives are introduced together, and the initial line of sight points in the direction of Mars’s normal eastward drift in the sky panel.
clips.narration: Here the two perspectives are shown side by side. On the left is the heliocentric view, and on the right is the night sky as seen from Earth.

clips.changeMeaning: The line of sight sweeps gradually in one direction and the Mars marker in the sky panel shifts correspondingly, linking orbital geometry to normal prograde motion.
clips.narration: As Earth moves toward the overtaking configuration, the line from Earth through Mars sweeps eastward across the background stars. In the sky view, Mars appears to drift eastward as well.

clips.changeMeaning: The line of sight reverses direction during the pass, and the Mars marker in the sky panel retraces westward, making the cause of retrograde visually direct.
clips.narration: During the overtaking itself, the line of sight reverses. At that same moment, Mars in the night-sky panel appears to move backward against the constellations.

components.text: Retrograde is apparent motion produced by real geometry

clips.changeMeaning: The line resumes its original sweep direction after Earth passes Mars, and the label now emphasizes that apparent motion is a genuine geometric effect rather than an observational illusion.
clips.narration: After Earth passes Mars, the line of sight resumes its eastward sweep and Mars resumes eastward drift. Retrograde is not a flaw in perception—it is a real apparent motion caused by changing geometry.

modules.description: Students use their own motion along a small floor orbit to generate an apparent retrograde shift of Mars against distant stars.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Experience retrograde motion as a perspective effect produced by observer motion.
Relate body movement around an inner track to Earth’s orbit around the Sun.
Use an analogy between planetary retrograde and overtaking in everyday life.
instructions: Stand near the marked floor orbit and imagine you are Earth.
As you move around the small circle, keep your eyes on the Mars marker ahead.
Notice when Mars seems to drift backward against the distant starfield as you pass the closest approach region.

components.text: Embodied model: You are Earth
Embodied model: You are Earth

clips.changeMeaning: The embodied analogy is introduced without moving the scene objects, focusing attention on the student’s own path as the source of changing perspective.
clips.narration: You can reproduce retrograde with your own motion. Imagine that you are Earth moving along the smaller, faster orbit while Mars remains farther away against a distant star background.

clips.changeMeaning: The floor orbit is visually highlighted to cue where students should walk, turning the diagram into a guided movement path.
clips.narration: Walk slowly around the marked circle while keeping your gaze fixed on Mars. The distant stars act like the much farther celestial background.

components.text: Near closest approach, Mars appears to drift backward

clips.changeMeaning: Instructional text now calls out the key overtaking phase and Mars is slightly emphasized so students know when to watch for the apparent backward shift.
clips.narration: As you pass the point of closest approach on your inner path, Mars appears to reverse against the distant stars. This is the same overtaking effect you experience when one car passes another on the highway.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Comparing Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn
modules.description: Students compare retrograde loop sizes for three outer planets and relate smaller loops to greater distance.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare the apparent retrograde loop sizes of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Explain why more distant planets show smaller loops.
Connect retrograde loop size to parallax-like angular geometry.
instructions: Observe Earth along with Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn in a heliocentric view.
Step through the highlighted retrograde event for each planet.
Compare the loop-size labels and relate them to each planet’s distance from Earth during overtaking.

components.text: Retrograde loop sizes: Mars > Jupiter > Saturn

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is highlighted first while the other outer planets are dimmed, establishing a clear focus for the initial comparison.
clips.narration: Outer planets all show retrograde motion, but not by the same amount. We begin with Mars, whose retrograde loop is the most dramatic of the three shown here.

components.text: Mars retrograde loop: about 15 degrees

clips.changeMeaning: The shared comparison label is updated to quantify Mars’s loop, connecting the highlighted planet to a concrete angular size.
clips.narration: Because Mars is relatively nearby during opposition, Earth’s changing viewpoint produces a loop about fifteen degrees across.

components.text: Jupiter retrograde loop: about 10 degrees

clips.changeMeaning: Attention shifts from Mars to Jupiter and the label updates accordingly, encouraging direct comparison of loop sizes with increasing distance.
clips.narration: Jupiter is farther away, so the same motion of Earth subtends a smaller angle. Its retrograde loop is typically closer to ten degrees.

components.text: Saturn retrograde loop: about 7 degrees

clips.changeMeaning: Focus shifts again to Saturn and the label quantifies the smallest loop, completing the ordered comparison across the three planets.
clips.narration: Saturn is farther still, so Earth’s motion changes the viewing angle even less. Its retrograde loop is smaller, around seven degrees.

components.text: Greater distance leads to smaller apparent shift

clips.changeMeaning: The final comparison label generalizes the planet-by-planet examples into a distance rule, reinforcing the parallax-style geometric explanation.
clips.narration: The pattern is the same idea as parallax: when you move, nearby objects shift more than distant ones. More distant outer planets therefore produce smaller retrograde loops.

modules.description: Students test whether they can place Mars in a configuration that produces retrograde motion as viewed from Earth.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict the orbital geometry associated with retrograde motion for Mars.
Use opposition and overtaking geometry to decide when retrograde should occur.
Differentiate productive relative positions from arbitrary absolute positions.
instructions: Drag Mars around its orbit and watch the Earth-view inset update.
Try to place Mars near the configuration where Earth is about to overtake it.
When the inset indicates retrograde, compare your placement to the opposition geometry.

components.scriptDescription: Allows Mars to be dragged around a fixed circular orbit around the Sun while keeping its orbital radius constant.

components.text: Place Mars where retrograde would be seen from Earth

clips.changeMeaning: The challenge begins with Earth fixed and Mars in a noncommittal starting position so students must reason from geometry rather than memorized coordinates.
clips.narration: Now you will predict when retrograde should occur. Earth is fixed on its orbit, and you can move Mars around its own orbit.

components.text: Hint: retrograde occurs near opposition, when Earth is poised to overtake Mars

clips.changeMeaning: The instructional label shifts from open-ended challenge to a targeted hint, scaffolding the student toward the relevant orbital configuration.
clips.narration: A useful clue is opposition. Retrograde happens when Mars is roughly opposite the Sun in Earth’s sky and Earth is near the point of overtaking it.

components.text: Correct region: line up Mars so Earth is about to pass it on the inside track

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is shown in a valid target arc, the inset is highlighted as a confirmation cue, and the label states the transferable geometric rule behind the successful placement.
clips.narration: When Mars is placed in this region, the Earth-view inset indicates retrograde. The key is not a special absolute location in space, but the relative geometry that puts Earth in position to pass Mars on the inside track.

modules.description: A closing summary reviews the major conceptual milestones of the lab in sequence.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize the observed pattern of retrograde motion.
Differentiate geocentric and heliocentric explanations.
Integrate observation, model, geometry, comparison, and prediction into a single coherent account.
instructions: Review each highlighted summary point as the narration recaps the lab.
Use Previous if you want to revisit any earlier guided scene before finishing.

components.text: 1. Observed loop in the sky
1. Observed phenomenon: eastward drift, westward loop, eastward return

clips.changeMeaning: The recap begins by restating the observational pattern, anchoring the synthesis in the concrete evidence students first encountered.
clips.narration: First, you saw the observed phenomenon itself: Mars drifts eastward, reverses into a westward loop, and then resumes eastward motion.

components.text: 2. Geocentric model: epicycles can fit the loop, but with added complexity

clips.changeMeaning: The summary advances to the historical geocentric explanation, preserving the timeline of ideas and its cost in complexity.
clips.narration: Second, you saw how the geocentric model used epicycles to reproduce the loop, but only with carefully tuned circles and speeds.

components.text: 3. Heliocentric model: Earth overtakes Mars on a faster inner orbit

clips.changeMeaning: The highlighted text now states the core heliocentric mechanism, transitioning from descriptive fit to causal explanation.
clips.narration: Third, the heliocentric model showed that Earth’s faster inner orbit naturally produces the retrograde episode when Earth overtakes Mars.

components.text: 4. Linked views and planet comparison: geometry sets loop size

clips.changeMeaning: The recap broadens from Mars alone to the cross-view geometric link and the distance dependence seen for Jupiter and Saturn.
clips.narration: Fourth, you linked the outside solar-system view to the night-sky view, and you compared Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn to see why more distant planets make smaller loops.

components.text: 5. Prediction: retrograde occurs near opposition, when relative geometry favors overtaking

clips.changeMeaning: The final recap point emphasizes prediction, ending the lab with a rule students can apply beyond the specific examples shown.
clips.narration: Finally, you used the geometry to predict when retrograde should occur. That predictive power is one reason the heliocentric explanation is preferred: it is both simpler and more powerful.
